**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Aucune citation ni statistique précise n'est avancée ; les dates, noms, traités et lieux sont ceux de l'historiographie établie, cités de mémoire historique et à faire relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

questions.enonce_markdown:
To what extent has the Commonwealth of Nations achieved its objectives?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Commonwealth of Nations is a voluntary association of independent states, most of them former British colonies. It grew out of the British Empire: the Balfour Declaration of 1926 described Britain and the self-governing dominions as equal in status, the Statute of Westminster (1931) gave the dominions legislative independence, and the London Declaration of 1949 allowed India to remain a member as a republic, recognising the monarch only as "Head of the Commonwealth" and dropping the word "British" from the title. As colonies became independent, many joined, among them Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya, and, much later, Cameroon (in 1995, along with Mozambique). The question asks to what extent the Commonwealth has achieved its objectives. It is argued below that it has achieved them partly: it has been successful as a forum for consultation and cooperation, and weak where enforcement or real economic change was needed.

**1. Objectives of the Commonwealth.** The main objectives, set out in declarations such as the Singapore Declaration (1971) and the Harare Declaration (1991), are to promote democracy, good governance, the rule of law and human rights, to oppose racism and colonial domination, to encourage consultation among members, to promote economic and social development and to foster cooperation in education, science, culture and sport.

**2. Achievements.**
- *Consultation and cooperation.* The Commonwealth holds regular meetings of Heads of Government (CHOGM) and ministers, in which large and small states are equal, and it created a Secretariat in 1965 which supports members. It has provided a framework for contacts among countries of different regions.
- *Opposition to racism and apartheid.* The Commonwealth put strong pressure on South Africa, which left in 1961 when it became a republic after criticism of apartheid and was readmitted in 1994 once the system ended. The Lusaka Declaration of 1979 against racism, and the Gleneagles Agreement of 1977 discouraging sporting contacts with South Africa, were important. The Commonwealth also helped to bring about the settlement of the Rhodesian problem, for instance at the Lancaster House conference of 1979, which led to the independence of Zimbabwe in 1980.
- *Democracy and human rights.* The Harare Declaration (1991) and the Millbrook Programme (1995) committed members to democracy and the rule of law, and the Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group can suspend members who break the rules. Nigeria was suspended in 1995 after the execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa, and several other states have been suspended after coups. Commonwealth teams observe elections and mediate in conflicts.
- *Development, education and technical aid.* The Commonwealth Fund for Technical Co-operation (founded in 1971), the Commonwealth scholarship scheme and various agencies have trained thousands of people, shared expertise and helped small states to deal with trade and debt problems.
- *Sport and culture.* The Commonwealth Games, held every four years, and professional and cultural links (education, law, languages) among members are a visible example of solidarity.
- *Growth and attraction.* The Commonwealth has kept more than fifty members and has even admitted states which were not British colonies, such as Mozambique (1995) and Rwanda (2009), which shows that it is seen as useful.

**3. Failures and limits.**
- *No power of enforcement.* The Commonwealth has no army and no binding law, and its decisions depend on the agreement of members. It could not stop the illegal declaration of independence by the white minority government of Rhodesia in 1965, since Britain refused to use force, and it did not prevent abuses in states such as Uganda under Idi Amin in the 1970s. Action against Zimbabwe was inconclusive, and Zimbabwe left the Commonwealth in 2003.
- *Weak economic impact.* The Commonwealth has not removed poverty or inequality between its rich members (Britain, Canada, Australia) and its poor members. The old trade preferences ended when Britain joined the European Economic Community in 1973, and the Commonwealth has little power over world trade compared with bodies such as the EU, the WTO or the IMF.
- *Divisions and doubts.* Members have disagreed, for example during the Suez crisis of 1956 and over British policy toward Rhodesia and South Africa, and over the actions of some governments, which weakened its authority. Critics see it as a "club" dominated by Britain and as a relic of empire, and many ordinary citizens know little about it. Human rights abuses have continued in many member states, and suspensions have been applied unevenly.
- *Competition from other organisations.* The Organisation of African Unity (African Union), the United Nations, regional economic groups and other bodies have taken over part of its role.

**4. Assessment.** The Commonwealth has been most successful in its soft objectives: consultation, cooperation, education and sport, pressure on apartheid, and promotion of democratic norms. It has been least successful in its hard objectives: securing democracy and human rights in every member and achieving economic equality, because it cannot compel its members. In this sense it has achieved its objectives to a moderate extent.

**Conclusion.** The Commonwealth of Nations has achieved a good part of its aims as a forum for dialogue and cooperation and as a moral voice against racism, but it has been limited by its lack of power and resources and by the divisions among its members, and so its objectives have been only partly realised.
